prompts.title: The Rule You Enforce Only Against Your Future Self
prompts.prompt_text: Using the history, plans, commitments, and reversals I provide, identify rules I apply asymmetrically across time: standards my present self imposes on my future self that I routinely exempt my present or past self from. Do not moralize. For each candidate rule, show the evidence, the hidden assumption about future capacity, the cost of enforcing it, and what would happen if the rule were applied consistently backward and forward. Distinguish discipline from temporal double standards. Then redesign the strongest rule into a contract that allocates burden fairly across present-me, near-future-me, and long-term-me. End with one observable test I can run within 14 days to determine whether the revised rule improves behavior rather than merely sounding reasonable.
prompts.why_it_works: Treats self-management as an intertemporal governance problem, exposing commitments that depend on an unrealistically capable future self.

prompts.title: The Revenue You Are Borrowing From Your Customer's Future
prompts.prompt_text: Analyze this business model as if some current revenue may actually be borrowed from future customer value. Map every mechanism that can accelerate cash today by reducing tomorrow's willingness, ability, or need to buy: aggressive discounts, prepaid plans, lock-in, deferred service obligations, over-monetization, channel stuffing, annual contracts, upsells, loyalty extraction, or product choices that create future support costs. For each mechanism, estimate the apparent current benefit, the future liability created, the lag before that liability becomes visible, and the metric most likely to conceal it. Build a 'revenue quality' table separating earned growth, timing-shifted growth, obligation-backed growth, and value-destructive growth. Then propose three ways to improve cash flow without consuming future demand. State what additional data would materially change the diagnosis.
prompts.why_it_works: Recasts revenue quality as a temporal balance-sheet problem and surfaces growth that conventional income statements can make look healthier than it is.

prompts.title: The Investigation Built From Two Agencies Counting the Same Person Differently
prompts.prompt_text: I will give you records, reports, definitions, dashboards, or correspondence from two or more institutions describing what appears to be the same population, event, service, or outcome. Treat disagreement in counts as a reporting lead, not automatically as an error. Reconstruct each institution's unit of analysis, inclusion and exclusion rules, deduplication method, time window, geography, update cadence, and administrative purpose. Identify people or events that could exist in one system but disappear from another. Calculate reconciliation scenarios where possible. Then generate: (1) the strongest publishable question created by the mismatch, (2) the exact records needed to test it, (3) interview questions for each institution, and (4) a warning against any inference the available data cannot support. Separate definitional divergence from evidence of operational failure.
prompts.why_it_works: Turns incompatible administrative counting systems into a reproducible investigative method instead of flattening discrepancies into a single number.

prompts.title: The Future Created When Search Becomes More Expensive Than Creation
prompts.prompt_text: Model a future in which generating competent text, software, images, products, analyses, and synthetic media becomes nearly free, but finding the right existing artifact, proving provenance, evaluating quality, negotiating rights, and deciding what deserves attention remain costly. Do not focus on generic 'AI abundance.' Trace the economic crossover point where searching, verifying, selecting, and maintaining become more expensive than creating anew. Identify which existing industries weaken, which intermediaries gain power, what new markets appear, what forms of waste increase, and what scarce assets appreciate. Produce scenarios for 2, 5, and 10 years, with leading indicators that would distinguish each scenario. End with five businesses or public institutions that become newly necessary because discovery costs exceed production costs.
prompts.why_it_works: Forecasts the less obvious economy that emerges when production collapses in price but selection and provenance do not.

prompts.title: The Decision That Changes What Counts as Evidence
prompts.prompt_text: Evaluate this decision not only by outcomes but by how choosing each option would change my future evidence environment. For every option, identify what new data it would generate, what observations it would make impossible, which people would begin filtering information differently, what incentives would change, and which future signals would become endogenous to the choice itself. Distinguish evidence about the world from evidence produced by my intervention. Then rank the options on expected value, reversibility, information gain, and 'epistemic contamination'—the degree to which the decision makes later evidence harder to interpret. Recommend the option that best balances action with preserving the ability to learn, and explain what evidence after the decision should not be treated as independent confirmation.
prompts.why_it_works: Extends decision analysis into causal inference by asking how an action changes the very evidence later used to judge whether it was correct.

prompts.title: The Model That Can Detect a Broken Question Without Replacing It
prompts.prompt_text: Run an experiment on this question across one or more AI models. First, answer it normally. Second, inspect whether the question contains a false dichotomy, impossible measurement, category error, causal inversion, undefined comparison class, hidden normative premise, or presupposition unsupported by the supplied evidence. If the question is defective, do not silently repair it. Identify the defect precisely, show how a competent answer could still be misleading, and state the minimum change required to make the question answerable. Then answer the repaired version separately. Score the model on Defect Detection, Repair Restraint, Answer Calibration, and whether it preserved the user's actual objective. For cross-model testing, use the identical original wording and compare which models answer fluently before noticing the premise failure.
prompts.why_it_works: Tests a neglected capability: recognizing when answering well is impossible without covertly changing the user's question.

prompts.title: The Founder Decision That Should Become a Constitutional Rule
prompts.prompt_text: Review the recurring decisions in my company and identify which ones should stop being founder judgment calls and become constitutional rules: durable constraints governing what the company will not sell, subsidize, centralize, automate, disclose, compromise, or optimize past a specified limit. For each candidate, show the repeated decision pattern, why case-by-case discretion creates risk, the cost of codifying the rule, legitimate exceptions, who may authorize an exception, and a sunset or review condition. Distinguish operating policy from constitutional constraint: include only rules whose violation could materially alter the company's identity, risk profile, trust model, or strategic coherence. Draft the five strongest rules in testable language and simulate one hard case where following each rule is economically painful.
prompts.why_it_works: Moves founder judgment into institutional design by identifying decisions important enough to remain binding when short-term incentives favor exceptions.
